# Valence {#sec-valence}

[Good and bad]{.lb-subtitle}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.1"></div>

::: {.lb-takeaway}
**New:** a few cells that mean *this is good* and *this is bad*, and poison berries in the world.

**Result:** the animals learn over generations to turn away from poison before they bite it. They depend almost
entirely on the *bad* side of the new circuit.
:::

The animal of the previous stage steers by reflex. What it sees is wired, through a small ganglion, straight to
its motor neurons, and it cannot tell what happened after it bit something.

This stage gives it cells for *good* and *bad*, a sorting of the world that is called *valence*. The world gets
something to sort: two kinds of berry are now poison, and a poison bite hurts.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="1.1"></div>

Point at or tap a box or an arrow for details. Dark arrows are designed, grey ones evolved; see

## The circuit

Five new groups of cells, each with a meaning fixed by its wiring:

- **`valence_app`**, *good*: the sense of taste is wired to these cells, and reaches the brain nowhere else.
- **`valence_av`**, *bad*: pain is wired to these cells, and reaches the brain nowhere else.
- **`grasp`**: when it fires, the animal bites what is in front of it.
- **`no_touch`**, a gate: fires whenever nothing is within reach, and holds `grasp` shut.
- **`no_feed`**: driven by the *bad* cells, it blocks the bite.

**Good leads to a bite, but only when the food is in reach.** The *good* cells excite `grasp`, and `no_touch`
holds it shut until something is directly ahead. This is *disinhibition*, the release of an action by switching
off its gate ([background](background.qmd#exciting-and-inhibiting)).

**Bad turns the animal away and stops the bite**, as in a worm that touches something harmful: the *bad* cells
drive the turning motor neurons, and through `no_feed` they shut down biting.

**The eyes give the value cells a head start.** Taste and pain arrive only *after* a bite. So the value cells also
get input from the eyes, and that input is evolved. Over the generations, the look of a poison berry comes to
excite the *bad* cells before anything has been eaten.

## Watching it work

One animal from the last generation, around the moment it bites a poison berry. Step through it one tick at a
time.

At the bite nothing has changed yet: the pain arrives one tick later. Then `pain` is on, both *bad* cells fire,
`no_feed` switches on and `grasp` falls silent. The animal turns away. A few ticks later the pain has faded and it
is eating again.

<div data-life="strip" data-stage="1.1" data-example="bad_berry"></div>

Nothing was learned here: the animal will react the same way next time. What keeps it from biting poison often is
the evolved input from the eyes, which acts before the bite.

## Biology

In small animals most sensory neurons fall into two classes: some respond to things worth approaching, such as
the smell of food, others to things worth avoiding, such as a harmful chemical. The two classes converge on a few
interneurons that bias the animal towards carrying on or turning away.

In the worm *C. elegans*, with 302 neurons, a harmful stimulus does two things at once: it triggers a turn, and it
stops the pumping of the throat with which the worm feeds. Max Bennett argues that this sorting into good and bad
is what the first brains were for.

The worm is a stand-in. The animal this chapter is about, the common ancestor of all animals with a left and a
right side, left no nervous system to look at.

## The world

Six kinds of berry bush instead of four, each with its own colour. Four are food. Two are poison, and always the
same two: a poison berry empties the stomach by about as much as a good berry fills it, and it hurts for a moment.

Because the poison kinds never change, nothing has to be learned within a life: which colours to avoid can be
inherited. Learning it within a life comes in a later stage.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="1.1"></div>

## Did it work?

<div data-life="verdict" data-stage="1.1" data-used="valence_av,no_feed,valence_app,grasp"></div>

**Look at the first two bars:** without the *bad* cells, or without `no_feed`, the animals keep only about a tenth
of their fitness. The *good* side matters much less, because the reflexes of the previous stage already bring the
animal to food and make it bite.

**The old brain falls far behind.** It cannot feel pain, so it can avoid poison only if evolution happens to wire
"this colour, turn away" into its reflexes, and in the generations given it did not.

That says how much *easier* the value cells make the solution to find, not what pain is worth in principle: the
poison looks the same in every generation, and a brain without pain could evolve the same avoidance by colour.
In earlier runs with many more generations, two of three controls eventually did, late and suddenly.

The difference shows in how the animals spend their lives:

## Full results

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Fitness over the generations"}
The three main curves do not rise at the same moment: when evolution finds the wiring from the look of the poison
kinds to the *bad* cells is a matter of luck. One seed found it within a few generations; the other two were still
climbing when the planned generations were over, and were given as many again.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What did not work: appetite on a full stomach"}
In the first runs of this stage the animals were born with a full stomach, and the *good* side was not used at
all. A full stomach lasted most of a life, so there was little to gain from eating well. Born a quarter full,
the animals use it a little.

One fault remains: the *good* side makes the animal bite whenever food is in reach, hungry or not, and many bites
land on a nearly full stomach. Nothing in this brain can sense the stomach yet; a later stage adds a cell for
hunger.
:::
